title: Find a Good Subset of the Matrix
statement:
`grid` is an `m x n` matrix of 0s and 1s whose rows are numbered from 0. Choose a non-empty set of `k` distinct rows; the choice is **good** when, in every column, the chosen rows hold at most `floor(k / 2)` ones in total.

Return the indices of the rows of a good choice, listed in increasing order. If several good choices exist, any one of them is accepted. If no good choice exists, return an empty array.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every set of rows is exponential. The key fact is that a good choice exists only if a tiny one does: either one row of all zeros, or two rows that never have a 1 in the same column.

Why: take a good choice of `k` rows. Each column holds at most `k / 2` ones, and there are at most 5 columns, so the chosen rows hold at most `2.5k` ones and some row has at most 2 ones. If it has none, it alone is good. Otherwise every other row that overlaps it must share one of its (at most 2) columns, and those columns leave room for at most `k - 2` other rows in total, fewer than the `k - 1` others, so some chosen row is disjoint from it.

With `n <= 5`, a row is a bitmask below 32, so only 32 distinct rows exist and every pair of them can be checked.

## Approach

1. Turn each row `i` into `mask`, setting bit `j` when `grid[i][j]` is 1.
2. If `mask` is 0, return `[i]` at once.
3. Remember the first row index for each mask in `firstRow`.
4. For every pair of stored masks, if `maskA & maskB` is 0, return the two row indices in increasing order.
5. Otherwise return an empty array.

## Example 1, step by step

Row 0 `[0,1,1,0]` becomes mask 6, row 1 `[0,0,0,1]` becomes 8, row 2 `[1,1,1,1]` becomes 15; none is 0. In the pair loop, `6 & 6` is not 0, but `6 & 8 = 0`, so the answer is `[0, 1]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m · n + 4^n): one pass builds the masks, then at most 32 × 32 pairs.
- Space: O(2^n) for `firstRow`.

## Pitfalls

- A pair of equal non-zero masks always overlaps; only distinct masks can work.
- Return the two indices in increasing order. A `Map` keeps insertion order, but a version that loops over the masks 0 to 31 meets the pair in mask order, which can put the later row first.
- An all-zero row is a full answer by itself; do not wait for a pair.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `mask` | row `i` as a bitmask of its 1 columns |
| `firstRow` | mask → first row index with that mask |
| `maskA`, `rowA` / `maskB`, `rowB` | the two candidate rows of a pair |

narration.2: Map each distinct row pattern to the first row that has it.
narration.4: Scan the rows once, top to bottom.
narration.5: Build this row's bitmask from scratch.
narration.6: Visit each of the at most 5 columns.
narration.7: Set bit j when the cell holds a 1.
narration.9: A row of all zeros is good on its own.
narration.10: Return it as a one-row answer.
narration.12: Only the first row with each pattern needs to be kept.
narration.17: Try every pair of distinct patterns that occur.
narration.18: Pair each pattern with every other stored pattern.
narration.19: Two rows with no shared 1 form a good pair: each column sums to at most 1.
narration.20: Return the pair's row indices in increasing order.
narration.24: No zero row and no disjoint pair means no good subset exists.
